readerTitle: The shop that keeps 55 cents and 2 cents of every dollar
caseNote: 가상 사례 (선물 가게, 장비 제조사의 부품팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 매출총이익률은 '상품이 돈을 버는가', 순이익률은 '사업 전체가 돈을 버는가'를 묻는다. 둘 사이의 간격이 어디를 고쳐야 할지 알려준다.
misconception: 마진은 하나의 숫자다. 매출총이익률이 높으면 사업도 잘되고 있다.

factChecks.note: 단순화를 위해 세금을 제외했습니다. 엄밀한 순이익률은 이자와 세금까지 뺀 값입니다. 7번 카드에서 이 점을 밝혔습니다.
소프트웨어의 매출총이익률이 대체로 높다는 서술과 슈퍼마켓·보석상 비교는 구체적 수치 없이 일반론으로만 썼습니다. 수치를 넣으려면 출처를 확인하세요.

cards.title: The shop that keeps 55 cents and 2 cents of every dollar
body: A gift shop owner buys a candle for $18 and sells it for $40. "I make 55% on everything," she tells a friend.
At year end, her accountant says the shop kept 2 cents of each dollar it took in. Both of them are telling the truth.

image.label: A candle on a shop counter with two price tags: 55% and 2%
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 작은 선물 가게 계산대. 양초 하나에 꼬리표 두 개가 달려 있음: 큰 꼬리표 "55%", 아주 작은 꼬리표 "2%". 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where do you look first?
body: The shop sells $400,000 a year. The goods it sold cost $180,000. After rent, staff and everything else, $8,000 is left.
The owner wants more profit. Where should she look first?

options.text: Find a cheaper supplier to push the 55% higher
options.feedback: It would help a little. But the products already earn a healthy 55%. Most of the money disappears later.

options.text: Look hard at the $212,000 of rent, staff and other costs
options.feedback: That's where 53 of every 55 cents go. The products work. The costs of running the shop are eating the result.
It might work, but it treats a running-cost problem as a price problem. If customers drift away, she loses both.

cards.title: Follow $100 of sales.
body: The first subtraction leaves **$55**. The second leaves **$2**. Two margins, two very different stories.

breakdown.label: Cost of goods
breakdown.detail: What the sold items cost to buy

cards.title: Gross margin vs net margin
body: **Gross margin** is sales minus the cost of the goods you sold, as a share of sales. It asks: does the product itself make money?
**Net margin** is what's left after every cost, as a share of sales. It asks: does the whole business make money?
The gap between them is the cost of running the business: rent, salaries, marketing, interest.

cards.title: Two margins, two different fixes.
body: Reading both numbers together tells you where to work.
list: **Low gross margin:** look at prices, suppliers, waste and which products you sell
**Healthy gross, low net:** look at rent, staff, marketing and other running costs
**Both low:** the product and the way you run it both need work
cards.callout: One margin tells you how you're doing. Two tell you where to look.
cards.softwareNote: Software gross margins are often high, because serving one more user costs little. Net margins can still be negative, because engineers, sales and marketing all sit below the gross line.

cards.title: A thin gross margin isn't always bad.
body: A supermarket earns little on each item. It survives because it sells huge volumes through the same rent and staff.
A jeweler needs a fat gross margin. It may sell a few pieces a day and still pays for a prime location, security and skilled staff.
So compare your margins with similar businesses, and with your own past. Comparing a grocer's gross margin with a jeweler's tells you nothing.

image.label: Two stacked bars: grocer and jeweler
image.brief: 막대 두 개 비교 일러스트. 왼쪽 "Grocer"는 매출총이익 층이 얇고, 오른쪽 "Jeweler"는 매출총이익 층이 두껍지만 운영비 층도 두꺼움. 두 막대 모두 맨 위 순이익 층은 비슷하게 얇음. 수치 없음, 실제 상호 없음.

cards.title: Where the line sits is a choice.
body: Businesses draw the gross line in different places. One shop counts delivery and packing as cost of goods. Another puts them under running costs. Same business, different gross margin.
Net margin moves with one-off items, interest and taxes, which we left out here to keep it simple. A single year can mislead. Check what's included before you compare, and look at several years.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You run the spare-parts team at an equipment maker. Finance reports your line at a 40% gross margin. After your share of head-office costs, its net margin is −3%.
An executive suggests closing the line. What do you say?

options.text: Agree. A negative net margin means it loses money
options.feedback: Much of the head-office share, like the main building and the finance team, stays if you close. You'd lose the 40% gross profit that helps pay for it.

options.text: Ask which costs below the gross line would actually disappear
options.feedback: This separates the product's own result from costs spread across every team. It tells you whether closing helps the company or just moves the costs.

options.text: Raise parts prices 15% to make the net margin positive
options.feedback: It may lift both margins, but it skips the real question. And loyal equipment customers may push back.

cards.title: Gross margin asks if the product pays. Net margin asks if the business pays.
body: Read them together. The gap between them shows what running the business costs.
**Try it today:** take last month's numbers. Work out your gross margin and your net margin, then write down the three biggest costs in the gap.
